title: "Nearby water use: old vs. new"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Run from the project root regardless of RStudio's knit-directory setting.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = here::here())
source("setup.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, dpi = 150)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Use NPS Park Tiles and the same 0-1 color scale for each comparison.
norm_map <- function(data, column, label) {
  mapview(data, zcol = column, layer.name = label, map.types = NULL,
          at = seq(0, 1, by = .2), col.regions = hcl.colors(100, "YlOrRd")) %>%
    add_nps_basemaps()
}
```

**Nearby-use exposure** measures future minus historical county withdrawals per
square kilometre (MGD/km2), representing change in surrounding demand pressure.
Higher values indicate larger increases; decreases retain negative raw values.

- **Old:** USGS/RPA withdrawals across six sectors; 2035–2065 minus the 1985–2015
average. P10/P50/P90 select the ensemble member nearest each percentile.
- **New:** Public supply, irrigation and thermoelectric withdrawals; 2040–2070
minus the 2000–2020 baseline. P10/P50/P90 report the model/pathway pair nearest
each absolute-change percentile; SSP1-2.6 is excluded.

Both use full 2020 TIGER/Line counties through `tigris`.

The two versions are not successive editions of one dataset. They are separate
studies that estimate county water use in fundamentally different ways, which is
why their results diverge as much as they do.

| | Old (Warziniack et al., 2022) | New (Blumberg and Warziniack) |
|---|---|---|
| Sectors | Six: domestic, industrial and mining, thermoelectric, irrigated agriculture, livestock, aquaculture | Three: public supply, crop irrigation, thermoelectric (~90% of US withdrawals) |
| Method | Structural accounting: each sector is a driver (population, income, irrigated acres, electricity generated) multiplied by a withdrawal rate (gallons per person, per dollar, per acre) | Reduced-form econometric panel on 2000–2020 observed withdrawals, with county-month and state-year fixed effects and county-specific time trends |
| Climate input | CMIP5 via MACA, 5 models x 4 SSP-RCP core scenarios (AR5 convention) | CMIP6, 7 models x 3 SSPs (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), 21 members after dropping SSP1-2.6 |
| Time resolution | Annual | Monthly, so seasonal climate response is estimated separately for each calendar month |
| Thermoelectric | Sector-level, driven by projected electricity generation | Plant-level, with cooling-type specific responses and climate averaged over transmission-constraint annuli (50–250 km) |
| Energy transition | Not represented | 24 states' clean-energy targets zero out coal and gas plants by their target dates; plants with no 2018–2020 withdrawals are treated as retired |
| Adaptation | Withdrawal rates follow assumed efficiency trajectories | Captured empirically by county time trends, with scenarios that relax them |

Three of these differences do most of the work. The **sector change** removes
livestock, aquaculture, and industrial and mining, so the new version is not
measuring the same quantity: counties whose demand is dominated by a dropped
sector shift position substantially. The **method change** replaces an accounting
identity with historically revealed climate responses, so the new estimates carry
observed behaviour and adaptation rather than assumed rates. The **energy
transition assumptions** are new, and they pull thermoelectric demand down
sharply (the paper reports -27.9% to -19.9% nationally) in exactly the counties
where the old version projected growing power-sector demand.

Those assumptions are worth stating plainly, because they are policy
projections rather than climate responses: the new estimates presume all 24
states meet their clean-energy targets. A county that loses its power plant
registers as a large decrease in nearby demand, which is a real reduction in
competition for water but one contingent on that policy outcome.

For both nearby-use versions and WTA exposure, signed absolute change is used
because percent change can exaggerate small changes when the baseline is low
and is undefined at a zero baseline. Percent change remains available for context;
the plots scale absolute changes to 0–1 after calculating county withdrawal
change per area or dimensionless WTA ratio change.

```{r calculate, include=FALSE}
sites <- get_wsd(rapid = TRUE)

water_supplies <- sites %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, park_unit, park_name, source_longitude, source_latitude) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("source_longitude", "source_latitude"), crs = 4326, na.fail = FALSE)

observed <- data.table::fread("data/all/RPAWaterDemand/1_BaseData/Trash 2022/usgswithdrawals.csv")

future <- data.table::fread("data/all/RPAWaterDemand/2_Demand_Results/cons_and_withdrawal.csv",
                            select = c("fips", "yearr", "scenario", "withdrawal"))

old <- calc_nearby_use_exposure_old(water_supplies, observed, future, verbose = FALSE) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(wsd_source_id, fips = if_else(is.na(fips), NA_character_, sprintf("%05d", as.integer(fips))),
            p90 = norm_absolute_use_change_p90, raw_p90 = raw_absolute_use_change_p90,
            data_status = NA_character_)

old_future_fips <- future %>% filter(between(yearr, 2035, 2065)) %>%
  distinct(fips) %>% pull(fips) %>% as.integer() %>% sprintf(fmt = "%05d")

rm(future)

new <- calc_nearby_use_exposure(water_supplies, verbose = FALSE) %>%
  transmute(wsd_source_id, fips, p90 = norm_absolute_use_change_p90,
            raw_p90 = raw_absolute_use_change_p90, data_status)

new_future_fips <- data.table::fread(
  "data/Latest county-level data/water_demand_projections/pub_irr_monthly_avg_2040_2070.csv",
  select = "FIPS") %>% distinct(FIPS) %>% pull(FIPS) %>% as.integer() %>% sprintf(fmt = "%05d")

pairs <- inner_join(old, new, by = "wsd_source_id", suffix = c("_old", "_new")) %>%
  filter(is.finite(p90_old), is.finite(p90_new)) %>%
  # Each version is min-max normalized over its own set of supplies, and a few
  # extreme old values squeeze the rest into a narrow band, so the normalized
  # scores are not comparable point-for-point. Rank the raw changes within the
  # shared set of supplies instead.
  mutate(rank_old = percent_rank(raw_p90_old), rank_new = percent_rank(raw_p90_new))

# Agreement between versions. Spearman is unaffected by min-max scaling.
agreement <- list(
  pearson = cor(pairs$p90_old, pairs$p90_new),
  spearman = cor(pairs$p90_old, pairs$p90_new, method = "spearman"),
  same_sign = mean(sign(pairs$raw_p90_old) == sign(pairs$raw_p90_new)),
  old_range = range(pairs$raw_p90_old),
  new_range = range(pairs$raw_p90_new),
  # How badly the old extremes compress the old normalized scale, and whether
  # ranking changes the sign of the apparent relationship.
  old_middle90 = unname(quantile(pairs$p90_old, c(.05, .95))),
  pearson_rank = cor(pairs$rank_old, pairs$rank_new))

wta <- calc_wta_exposure(water_supplies, huc_level = 8L, verbose = FALSE) %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, huc, raw_wta_change_p90, norm_wta_change_p90)
wta_distribution <- wta %>%
  distinct(huc, raw_wta_change_p90, norm_wta_change_p90) %>%
  filter(is.finite(norm_wta_change_p90))
wta_range <- range(wta_distribution$raw_wta_change_p90)
wta_middle <- quantile(wta_distribution$norm_wta_change_p90, c(.05, .95))
wta_zero <- scales::rescale(0, from = wta_range)
waterrights <- calc_waterrights_exposure(
  water_supplies,
  stress_data = here("data", "rapid", "inputs", "WaterRightsIndicator",
                     "waterrights_stress_long.csv"),
  period = "2050", verbose = FALSE) %>%
  select(wsd_source_id, norm_water_stress_2050)

map_data <- water_supplies %>%
  left_join(pairs %>% select(wsd_source_id, p90_old, p90_new), by = "wsd_source_id")
wta_rights_map_data <- water_supplies %>%
  left_join(wta, by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
  left_join(waterrights, by = "wsd_source_id")
```

```{r missing-sites, include=FALSE}
# Classify why each supply has no result.
missing_sites <- function(results, future_fips) {
  results %>%
    filter(!is.finite(p90)) %>%
    left_join(select(sites, wsd_source_id, park_name, water_system_name), by = "wsd_source_id") %>%
    arrange(park_name, water_system_name, wsd_source_id) %>%
    transmute(Park = park_name, `Water system` = water_system_name,
              `Source ID` = wsd_source_id, `County FIPS` = fips,
              Gap = case_when(is.na(fips) ~ "No county FIPS match",
                              !fips %in% future_fips ~ "County absent from future file",
                              !is.na(data_status) ~ str_to_sentence(gsub("_", " ", data_status)),
                              TRUE ~ "Unavailable result"))
}
missing_new <- missing_sites(new, new_future_fips)
missing_old <- missing_sites(old, old_future_fips)

missing_both <- missing_new %>% filter(`Source ID` %in% missing_old$`Source ID`)
missing_new_only <- missing_new %>% filter(!`Source ID` %in% missing_old$`Source ID`)
missing_old_only <- missing_old %>% filter(!`Source ID` %in% missing_new$`Source ID`)

historical_new_fips <- data.table::fread(
  "data/Latest county-level data/water_demand_projections/pub_irr_monthly_avg_2000_2020.csv",
  select = "FIPS") %>%
  transmute(FIPS = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS))) %>%
  distinct()
future_new_fips <- data.table::fread(
  "data/Latest county-level data/water_demand_projections/pub_irr_monthly_avg_2040_2070.csv",
  select = "FIPS") %>%
  transmute(FIPS = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS))) %>%
  distinct()
missing_county_fips <- anti_join(historical_new_fips, future_new_fips, by = "FIPS")

missing_counties <- tigris::counties(cb = FALSE, year = 2020, progress_bar = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(FIPS = GEOID) %>%
  filter(FIPS %in% missing_county_fips$FIPS) %>%
  mutate(coverage = "Historical only")
```

### Supplies without results

`r nrow(missing_new)` supplies have no new nearby-use exposure result and
`r nrow(missing_old)` have no old result. `r nrow(missing_both)` are missing
from both versions, in `r n_distinct(missing_both$"County FIPS")` counties whose
codes are absent from the future file in both datasets. `r nrow(missing_new_only)`
are missing only from the new version, in
`r n_distinct(missing_new_only$"County FIPS")` counties with incomplete future
thermoelectric plant records (a known plant has no projection, so the future
total is unavailable rather than assumed zero). `r nrow(missing_old_only)` are
missing only from the old version.

```{r missing-sites-table}
knitr::kable(missing_new)
```

The plot compares the two versions by percentile rank of
`raw_absolute_use_change_p90`: signed withdrawal change per county area, ranked
within the supplies that have both results. Ranking rather than plotting the
normalized scores keeps the comparison honest. Each version is min-max scaled
over its own set of supplies, and a handful of extreme old values pin the ends
of the old scale: 90% of old normalized scores fall between
`r round(agreement$old_middle90[1], 2)` and `r round(agreement$old_middle90[2], 2)`,
a span of just `r round(diff(agreement$old_middle90), 2)` of the 0–1 range.
Plotted that way the points form a tight vertical band that reflects the scaling
rather than the relationship. Each point is a supply with both results; the
dashed line marks equal rank.

```{r}
ggplotly(ggplot(pairs, aes(rank_old, rank_new)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "grey55") +
  geom_point(alpha = .45, color = "#2166AC") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  # ggplotly drops subtitles, so the supply count goes in the title.
  labs(title = paste0("Percentile rank of P90 change in county withdrawals (",
                      nrow(pairs), " supplies with both results)"),
       x = "Old: percentile rank", y = "New: percentile rank"))
```

### Spatial comparison

The maps below show where the two versions disagree. Given the differences set
out above, the disagreement is expected rather than a sign that one version is
wrong: the versions cover different sectors, estimate demand by different means,
and make different assumptions about the power sector. Weak agreement is the
result of comparing two genuinely different estimates of county water use, not
of a processing error in either.

The two versions agree only weakly. Across the `r nrow(pairs)` supplies with
both results, the rank (Spearman) correlation of P90 change is
`r round(agreement$spearman, 2)`, and both versions show the same direction of
change for `r scales::percent(agreement$same_sign)` of supplies. The Pearson
correlation of the normalized scores is `r round(agreement$pearson, 2)`, pulled
down by a few extreme old values: old raw P90 change ranges from
`r signif(agreement$old_range[1], 2)` to `r signif(agreement$old_range[2], 2)`
MGD/km2, versus `r signif(agreement$new_range[1], 2)` to
`r signif(agreement$new_range[2], 2)` for the new version. Those extremes are
also why the rank plot above is the fair comparison, and the reason matters:
the Pearson correlation of the normalized scores is negative while the rank
correlation is positive (`r round(agreement$pearson_rank, 2)`). A plot of
normalized scores would therefore suggest the two versions run in opposite
directions, when in fact they agree weakly but positively. Ranked, the points
spread across the square along a loose diagonal, which is the agreement the
Spearman correlation actually reports.

The synchronized maps share the same 0–1 color scale.

```{r nearby-use-maps}
m_old <- norm_map(map_data %>% filter(is.finite(p90_old)), "p90_old",
                  "Old nearby use P90 (normalized)")
m_new <- norm_map(map_data %>% filter(is.finite(p90_new)), "p90_new",
                  "New nearby use P90 (normalized)")
leafsync::sync(m_old, m_new, ncol = 2)
```

Both the original and new water-use datasets have inconsistent county coverage
between their historical and future files. Many counties that appear in the 
historical data, especially Virginia counties and independent cities, are missing
from the future projections, while the original dataset also contains some 
future-only county codes. This suggests a county FIPS or county-equivalent 
crosswalk problem during data preparation rather than a true absence of water 
use. Because the missing counties cannot be matched confidently across periods,
their future changes are flagged as unavailable instead of being treated as zero.

```{r wta-coverage-gap, include=FALSE}
# The same historical-vs-future coverage mismatch, at HUC8 in the WTA files.
wta_dir <- "data/Latest county-level data/water_demand_projections"
wta_hist_huc <- data.table::fread(file.path(wta_dir, "wta_ratios_2000_2020.csv"),
                                  select = c("huc", "agg")) %>%
  filter(agg == "HUC08") %>% distinct(huc) %>% pull(huc)
wta_future_huc <- data.table::fread(file.path(wta_dir, "wta_ratios_2040_2070.csv"),
                                    select = c("huc", "agg")) %>%
  filter(agg == "HUC08") %>% distinct(huc) %>% pull(huc)
wta_gap_huc <- setdiff(wta_hist_huc, wta_future_huc)
wta_gap_sites <- wta %>% filter(!is.finite(raw_wta_change_p90))
```

The WTA ratios carry the same kind of gap one level up. Of the
`r length(wta_hist_huc)` HUC8 watersheds in the historical file,
`r length(wta_gap_huc)` (`r paste(wta_gap_huc, collapse = ", ")`) is absent from
the projections, leaving `r nrow(wta_gap_sites)` supplies without a WTA exposure
result. WTA sensitivity is unaffected, since it reads only the historical file.
As with the counties above, the gap is treated as unavailable rather than as no
change. It is worth noting alongside the county gaps because both originate in
the same upstream dataset: a spatial unit present in the baseline and missing
from the future projections, rather than a genuine absence of water use.

The first map shows every supply without a new result, colored by the reason,
with county boundaries within 200 km. The second shows all historical counties
absent from the new future projection file.

```{r missing-sites-map}
missing_site_points <- sites %>%
  select(wsd_source_id) %>%
  inner_join(select(missing_new, wsd_source_id = `Source ID`, Gap), by = "wsd_source_id")

site_buf <- missing_site_points %>%
  st_transform(5070) %>%
  st_buffer(200000)

counties <- tigris::counties(cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(site_buf)) %>%
  filter(lengths(st_intersects(., site_buf)) > 0)

add_nps_basemaps(
  mapview(missing_site_points, zcol = "Gap", layer.name = "Supplies without a new result",
          map.types = NULL) +
    mapview(counties, layer.name = "Counties", alpha.regions = 0, map.types = NULL))
```

```{r missing-county-map}
mapview(missing_counties,
        map.types = NULL,
        zcol = "coverage",
        layer.name = "Historical counties absent from future file",
        col.regions = "#D73027",
        alpha.regions = 0.6,
        color = "white") %>%
  add_nps_basemaps()
```

### WTA and water-rights exposure

**WTA exposure** measures change in the withdrawal-to-modeled-runoff ratio from
2000–2020 to 2040–2070 at HUC8, using the actual ensemble member nearest P90;
SSP1-2.6 is excluded. Higher values indicate greater worsening of water stress.

**WTA sensitivity** is the historical 2000–2020 HUC8 ratio, with higher values
indicating greater existing stress. It has one historical value per watershed,
so no percentile is selected; sensitivity is not plotted here.

**Water-rights exposure** is the highest projected 2050 Aqueduct stress score
across pathways at HydroBASINS Level 6. These maps share a 0–1 color scale but
compare projected stress level with WTA's change in stress.

```{r wta-water-rights-map}
m_wta <- norm_map(wta_rights_map_data %>% filter(is.finite(norm_wta_change_p90)),
                  "norm_wta_change_p90", "HUC8 WTA P90 change (normalized)")
m_rights <- norm_map(wta_rights_map_data %>% filter(is.finite(norm_water_stress_2050)),
                     "norm_water_stress_2050", "Water rights 2050 (normalized)")
leafsync::sync(m_wta, m_rights, ncol = 2)
```

Min–max normalization scales the raw P90 WTA changes from `r round(wta_range[1], 2)`
to `r round(wta_range[2], 2)` into 0–1. The extremes compress most scores:
90% of represented HUC8 values lie between `r round(wta_middle[1], 3)` and
`r round(wta_middle[2], 3)`. The histogram counts each HUC8 once; its dashed line
marks zero raw change (normalized `r round(wta_zero, 3)`).

```{r wta-histogram}
ggplot(wta_distribution, aes(norm_wta_change_p90)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .02, boundary = 0, fill = "#2166AC", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = wta_zero, linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of normalized P90 WTA change",
       x = "Normalized HUC8 P90 WTA change", y = "HUC8 watersheds")
```
